Generalized policy iteration: judge, improve, repeat

The loop of evaluation and improvement inside most reinforcement learning methods, worked through on the cliff grid and traced from dynamic programming to AlphaGo Zero.

October 23, 202616 min read

reinforcement-learningmachine-learning

Let's go back to the cliff grid from Part 1 of my RL series: 4 rows by 12 columns, a start S at the bottom left, a flag G at the bottom right and ten cliff cells between them. Every move gives a reward of −1, a step into the cliff gives −100 and sends you back to S, a move into the outer wall leaves you where you are, and later costs count a little less, with a discount of γ = 0.99. In Part 1, Q-learning found the best route by trial and error. This time, suppose you know the rules of the grid exactly. You know where every move leads and what it costs. Can you just work out the best way to move?

You could try every rule. A rule here picks one move in each of the 37 cells where you have to choose (the flag ends the episode), so there are 437≈1.9×10224^{37} \approx 1.9 \times 10^{22}437≈1.9×1022 of them. That's far too many. What you want instead is a way to take one rule and make it better. But to know whether a change helps, you need to know what the current rule earns from each cell, and that depends on every move the rule makes after that cell. So the two questions, "how good is this rule?" and "what's a better rule?", chase each other: you can't improve a rule without judging it, and every improvement changes what you have to judge.

The answer is to alternate between them. The idea is simple, and once you see it, you'll find it inside almost every reinforcement learning method, all the way up to AlphaGo Zero.

This is a side article to my reinforcement learning series. It follows Chapter 4 of Sutton and Barto's book, and every book page number below refers to its second edition.

How good is the current rule?

Let's start with the worst reasonable rule: a random walker that picks each of the four moves with chance ¼. A rule for choosing moves is called a policy, written π\piπ, and π(a∣s)\pi(a \mid s)π(a∣s) is the chance it picks move aaa in cell sss.

The return GtG_tGt​ is what you collect from step ttt on, with each later reward discounted once more: Gt=Rt+1+γRt+2+γ2Rt+3+⋯G_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t+2} + \gamma^2 R_{t+3} + \cdotsGt​=Rt+1​+γRt+2​+γ2Rt+3​+⋯. The value of a cell under a policy, vπ(s)v_\pi(s)vπ​(s), is the return you get on average when you start in sss and follow π\piπ. Computing vπv_\pivπ​ for a given policy is called policy evaluation, or the prediction problem (§4.1, p. 74).

The value of a cell depends on the values of the cells you can reach in one move. The book writes this as the Bellman equation for vπv_\pivπ​ (eq. 4.4, p. 74):

vπ(s)=∑aπ(a∣s)∑s′,rp(s′,r∣s,a) [r+γ vπ(s′)]v_\pi(s) = \sum_a \pi(a \mid s) \sum_{s', r} p(s', r \mid s, a)\,\big[r + \gamma\, v_\pi(s')\big] vπ​(s)=a∑​π(a∣s)s′,r∑​p(s′,r∣s,a)[r+γvπ​(s′)]

Here p(s′,r∣s,a)p(s', r \mid s, a)p(s′,r∣s,a) is the chance that move aaa in cell sss lands in cell s′s's′ with reward rrr. That's the model of the grid, and here you know it. In words: average over the moves the policy picks and over where each one lands, then add the reward to the discounted value of the next cell. On this grid every move has a single outcome, so the inner sum has just one term. There's one equation per cell, so for this grid you get 37 linear equations with 37 unknowns.

The first panel shows the answer. The random walker's values run from about −482, in the cell above the flag, down to −1072 at S: one move in four from S steps straight into the cliff, and the walker takes a long time to stumble onto the flag.

Two ways to solve for the values

You can solve the 37 equations directly, which is what the script for this article does. Or you can sweep through the cells and replace each value with the right-hand side, using the current guesses for the next cells (eq. 4.5, p. 74):

vk+1(s)=∑aπ(a∣s)∑s′,rp(s′,r∣s,a)[r+γ vk(s′)]\begin{aligned} v_{k+1}(s) &= \sum_a \pi(a \mid s) \sum_{s', r} p(s', r \mid s, a) \\ &\qquad \big[r + \gamma\, v_k(s')\big] \end{aligned} vk+1​(s)​=a∑​π(a∣s)s′,r∑​p(s′,r∣s,a)[r+γvk​(s′)]​

With γ<1\gamma < 1γ<1, these sweeps converge to vπv_\pivπ​ in the limit, from any starting guess that gives the flag a value of 0 (pp. 74-75). That second form matters later, because you can stop the sweeps early.

Act greedily on those numbers

Now let's use the values to pick better moves. For each move aaa in cell sss, ask what you'd get if you made that move once and then went back to following π\piπ. That's the action value (eq. 4.6, p. 78):

qπ(s,a)=∑s′,rp(s′,r∣s,a) [r+γ vπ(s′)]q_\pi(s, a) = \sum_{s', r} p(s', r \mid s, a)\,\big[r + \gamma\, v_\pi(s')\big] qπ​(s,a)=s′,r∑​p(s′,r∣s,a)[r+γvπ​(s′)]

Then, in every cell, pick the move with the highest action value. This is the greedy policy (eq. 4.9, p. 79):

π′(s)=arg⁡max⁡aqπ(s,a)\pi'(s) = \arg\max_a q_\pi(s, a) π′(s)=argamax​qπ​(s,a)

Here π′(s)\pi'(s)π′(s) is a single move, not a probability. Changing the policy this way is called policy improvement. Panel 2 shows what one greedy step does to the random walker. On the right side of the grid, the white arrows all reach the flag, some by way of the top row. On the left side, every cell near the cliff looks so bad that the greedy move is to go up and away from it. The ten red cells in the left three columns all get funnelled into the top-left corner. That corner has the walker's best value on that side, −929, so its greedy move is to stay put by bumping into the top wall, forever. That costs −1 per step, which adds up to −1/(1−γ)=−100-1/(1-\gamma) = -100−1/(1−γ)=−100.

So the new policy is silly: it never reaches the flag from S. And yet no cell got worse. S went from −1072 to −100, and every one of the 37 cells improved.

That's not luck. The policy improvement theorem (eq. 4.7 and 4.8, p. 78) says that if, in every cell, making the new policy's move once and then following the old policy is at least as good as following the old policy all the way,

qπ(s,π′(s))≥vπ(s)for every s,q_\pi(s, \pi'(s)) \ge v_\pi(s) \quad \text{for every } s, qπ​(s,π′(s))≥vπ​(s)for every s,

then the new policy is at least as good everywhere: vπ′(s)≥vπ(s)v_{\pi'}(s) \ge v_\pi(s)vπ′​(s)≥vπ​(s) for every sss. Why does that hold? If switching to π′\pi'π′ for one move doesn't hurt, you can make the same switch at the next cell, and the one after that. Each switch can only add value, and switching at every step is just following π′\pi'π′. After kkk switches, all that's left of the old policy is γkvπ(St+k)\gamma^k v_\pi(S_{t+k})γkvπ​(St+k​), which shrinks to zero.

The greedy policy always meets that condition. The old policy's value is the average of its action values, vπ(s)=∑aπ(a∣s) qπ(s,a)v_\pi(s) = \sum_a \pi(a \mid s)\, q_\pi(s, a)vπ​(s)=∑a​π(a∣s)qπ​(s,a), and the best action value is at least that average.

The full proof chain (p. 78)

Start from the condition and unroll it one step at a time:

vπ(s)≤qπ(s,π′(s))=E[Rt+1+γvπ(St+1)∣St=s,At=π′(s)]=Eπ′[Rt+1+γvπ(St+1)∣St=s]≤Eπ′[Rt+1+γqπ(St+1,π′(St+1))∣St=s]=Eπ′[Rt+1+γRt+2+γ2vπ(St+2)∣St=s]≤Eπ′[Rt+1+γRt+2+γ2Rt+3+γ3vπ(St+3)∣St=s]    ⋮≤Eπ′[Rt+1+γRt+2+γ2Rt+3+γ3Rt+4+⋯∣St=s]=vπ′(s)\begin{aligned} v_\pi(s) &\le q_\pi(s, \pi'(s)) \\ &= \mathbb{E}\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma v_\pi(S_{t+1}) \mid S_t = s, A_t = \pi'(s)\big] \\ &= \mathbb{E}_{\pi'}\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma v_\pi(S_{t+1}) \mid S_t = s\big] \\ &\le \mathbb{E}_{\pi'}\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma q_\pi(S_{t+1}, \pi'(S_{t+1})) \mid S_t = s\big] \\ &= \mathbb{E}_{\pi'}\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t+2} + \gamma^2 v_\pi(S_{t+2}) \mid S_t = s\big] \\ &\le \mathbb{E}_{\pi'}\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t+2} + \gamma^2 R_{t+3} + \gamma^3 v_\pi(S_{t+3}) \mid S_t = s\big] \\ &\;\;\vdots \\ &\le \mathbb{E}_{\pi'}\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t+2} + \gamma^2 R_{t+3} + \gamma^3 R_{t+4} + \cdots \mid S_t = s\big] \\ &= v_{\pi'}(s) \end{aligned} vπ​(s)​≤qπ​(s,π′(s))=E[Rt+1​+γvπ​(St+1​)∣St​=s,At​=π′(s)]=Eπ′​[Rt+1​+γvπ​(St+1​)∣St​=s]≤Eπ′​[Rt+1​+γqπ​(St+1​,π′(St+1​))∣St​=s]=Eπ′​[Rt+1​+γRt+2​+γ2vπ​(St+2​)∣St​=s]≤Eπ′​[Rt+1​+γRt+2​+γ2Rt+3​+γ3vπ​(St+3​)∣St​=s]⋮≤Eπ′​[Rt+1​+γRt+2​+γ2Rt+3​+γ3Rt+4​+⋯∣St​=s]=vπ′​(s)​

Eπ′\mathbb{E}_{\pi'}Eπ′​ means the average over what happens when you follow π′\pi'π′. Each ≤\le≤ uses the condition at the next cell. The random walker is a stochastic policy, and the theorem covers that case too (p. 79).

Repeat until nothing changes

The values you hold still belong to the old policy, so they're wrong for the new one. Evaluate again, then improve again. That alternation is policy iteration (§4.3, p. 80):

π0→  E  vπ0→  I  π1→  E  vπ1→  I  π2→  E  ⋯→  I  π∗→  E  v∗\begin{aligned} &\pi_0 \xrightarrow{\;E\;} v_{\pi_0} \xrightarrow{\;I\;} \pi_1 \xrightarrow{\;E\;} v_{\pi_1} \xrightarrow{\;I\;} \pi_2 \\ &\xrightarrow{\;E\;} \cdots \xrightarrow{\;I\;} \pi_* \xrightarrow{\;E\;} v_* \end{aligned} ​π0​E​vπ0​​I​π1​E​vπ1​​I​π2​E​⋯I​π∗​E​v∗​​

Here E is a full evaluation and I is a greedy improvement. On the cliff grid it takes six rounds, shown in panel 3. Rounds 2 and 3 free the stuck cells a column at a time, since a stuck cell only switches once a neighbor has a better value to offer, but S stays at −100. In round 4, S finally finds a 17-step route: three cells along the cliff edge, then up to the top row and along it (yellow, −15.71). In round 6 the route drops down to the cliff edge: up once, right eleven times, down onto the flag, 13 steps (green, −12.25). That's the route Q-learning found in Part 1, and −12.25 is the same score its table gave "up" from S.

After round 6, one more greedy step changes nothing, so the loop stops. That's also why the final policy is optimal. If no single move beats the policy's own move in any cell, even when you judge the moves by the policy's own values, then those values satisfy the Bellman optimality equation, and only the optimal values v∗v_*v∗​ do (pp. 64 and 79). The loop also has to stop. With the tie rule in the drawer below, a round only changes a move when the new move is strictly better, so at least one cell gets strictly better (p. 78) and no policy can come back. And there are only finitely many deterministic policies, the ones that pick a single move in each cell (p. 80).

In practice it stops much faster than the count of policies suggests: 6 rounds here, out of 1.9×10221.9 \times 10^{22}1.9×1022 possible policies.

Every round on the grid
Round v(S) Moves changed Cells improved
0 (random) −1072.24
1 −100.00 all 37 37
2 −100.00 6 6
3 −100.00 5 5
4 −15.71 5 6
5 −15.71 2 2
6 −12.25 2 9

No cell's value ever goes down from one round to the next. When two moves tie, the policy keeps its current move, so the loop can't flip between equally good moves forever (p. 80; Exercise 4.4, p. 82). The first greedy step from the random walker breaks ties in the order up, right, down, left. Every other order gives the same values and the same counts. Evaluation solves the linear equations exactly. To reproduce the numbers and the drawing, run python3 scripts/rl_gpi_figures.py in the site's repository.

Why a stable policy is optimal

If the greedy step changes nothing, then π′\pi'π′ is as good as π\piπ, so vπ′=vπv_{\pi'} = v_\pivπ′​=vπ​, and the greedy step gives, for every cell,

vπ′(s)=max⁡a∑s′,rp(s′,r∣s,a) [r+γ vπ′(s′)]v_{\pi'}(s) = \max_a \sum_{s', r} p(s', r \mid s, a)\,\big[r + \gamma\, v_{\pi'}(s')\big] vπ′​(s)=amax​s′,r∑​p(s′,r∣s,a)[r+γvπ′​(s′)]

That's the Bellman optimality equation (eq. 4.1, p. 73). For a finite problem like this one, its only solution is v∗v_*v∗​, the best value any policy can reach (p. 64), so vπ′=v∗v_{\pi'} = v_*vπ′​=v∗​ and π′\pi'π′ is optimal (p. 79).

Two processes, any amount of work

Policy iteration finishes each process before starting the other: evaluate all the way, then improve every cell. But you don't have to. Value iteration stops evaluation after a single sweep, one update of every cell from the current guesses of its neighbors, and takes the max right inside it (eq. 4.10, p. 83):

vk+1(s)=max⁡a∑s′,rp(s′,r∣s,a) [r+γ vk(s′)]v_{k+1}(s) = \max_a \sum_{s', r} p(s', r \mid s, a)\,\big[r + \gamma\, v_k(s')\big] vk+1​(s)=amax​s′,r∑​p(s′,r∣s,a)[r+γvk​(s′)]

On the cliff grid, starting from all zeros, value iteration reaches the exact optimal values at sweep 14, and sweep 15 changes nothing. Asynchronous methods go even finer: they can update one cell at a time, in any order, and with γ<1\gamma < 1γ<1 they still converge as long as every cell keeps getting updated (§4.5, p. 85).

Sutton and Barto call the general idea generalized policy iteration, or GPI: "letting policy-evaluation and policy-improvement processes interact, independent of the granularity and other details of the two processes" (§4.6, p. 86). Panel 4 redraws their diagram. Evaluation pulls V, the current value estimate, toward vπv_\pivπ​, the true values of the current policy. Improvement pulls the policy toward greedy(V). With full evaluation and fully greedy improvement, the loop can only settle at an optimal policy π∗\pi_*π∗​ and the optimal value v∗v_*v∗​, because that's the only place where both processes stop changing anything (p. 86).

And here's the claim that makes it worth learning: "Almost all reinforcement learning methods are well described as GPI" (p. 86).

Two goals that pull apart

The book's second diagram (p. 87) draws the two goals as two lines. Think of each point as a pair: a value table vvv and a policy π\piπ. On the blue line, the values are right for the policy: v=vπv = v_\piv=vπ​. On the green line, the policy is greedy for the values: π=greedy(v)\pi = \text{greedy}(v)π=greedy(v). Each step of policy iteration jumps all the way onto one line, and that jump usually knocks you off the other: new values can make a different move look best, and a new policy makes the old values wrong. Still, the zigzag climbs to the point where the lines meet.

The authors say the two processes "can be viewed as both competing and cooperating" (p. 86). You can see both on the cliff grid. Round 1's greedy step made the random walker's values wrong: the top-left corner was worth −929 to the walker and −100 to the new policy. Then evaluation fixed the values, and the policy was no longer greedy for them in 6 cells. Each step undoes the other's work. Even so, S's value never drops, and the loop ends at the optimum.

The book adds that the real geometry is "much more complicated" than two lines (p. 87). So the drawing helps you think about the loop, but it isn't a map of all possible value tables and policies.

The same loop inside other methods

When you know the rules of the world, both processes can use them. But most RL methods don't know the rules, so they replace each process with something they can do from experience. Panel 6 lists what plays each role.

  • Monte Carlo control (§5.2-5.3, pp. 96-99) evaluates by averaging the returns of whole episodes. Without a model, the values of cells alone can't tell you which move is best, because turning vvv into qqq needs ppp (p. 96), so it learns action values Q(s,a)Q(s,a)Q(s,a) and, after each episode, acts greedily on them in the cells it visited. That only works if every move keeps getting tried, so the book's version, Monte Carlo ES, starts each episode from a random cell and move (pp. 98-99).
  • Sarsa (§6.4, p. 129) follows "the pattern of generalized policy iteration (GPI), only this time using TD methods for the evaluation or prediction part". Each step nudges Q(s,a)Q(s,a)Q(s,a) toward one reward plus the next estimate, a temporal-difference (TD) update, and the policy is ε-greedy on QQQ, so improvement happens at every step.
  • Q-learning (§6.5, p. 131) puts the max inside its update target, R+γmax⁡aQ(S′,a)R + \gamma \max_a Q(S', a)R+γmaxa​Q(S′,a), so improvement happens inside every evaluation update. The book's chart of one-step updates (Figure 8.6, p. 172) pairs it with value iteration on action values, using one sampled next cell instead of an average over all of them. Section 6.5 doesn't mention GPI itself; the book covers it with a chapter-wide claim that DP, TD and Monte Carlo methods "all use some variation of generalized policy iteration (GPI)" (p. 119).
  • Actor-critic methods (§13.5, p. 331) split the two roles into two parts. The critic learns state values with TD errors, and the actor is the policy, nudged by a gradient step toward what the critic favors. The book says the critic "uses a TD method to evaluate the actor's policy", with its estimates "allowing the actor to improve its policy" (p. 346). But it never calls actor-critic GPI, and on p. 460 it even lists the two as separate ways to learn a policy. The SAC paper is more direct: "Actor-critic algorithms are typically derived starting from policy iteration" (Haarnoja et al., 2018, p. 2).
  • AlphaGo Zero: in their case study, Sutton and Barto write that "AlphaGo Zero implemented a form of policy iteration (Section 4.3), interleaving policy evaluation with policy improvement" (§16.6.2, p. 447).

The AlphaGo Zero paper (Silver et al., 2017) says the same. A neural network outputs move probabilities ppp and a value vvv for a board. A tree search (Monte Carlo tree search, MCTS) guided by that network returns search probabilities π\piπ that "usually select much stronger moves than the raw move probabilities p of the neural network fθ(s)f_\theta(s)fθ​(s); MCTS may therefore be viewed as a powerful policy improvement operator". Self-play with search, "using the game winner z as a sample of the value", "may be viewed as a powerful policy evaluation operator". Then the network is trained toward both, its value vvv toward the winner zzz (evaluation) and its move probabilities ppp toward π\piπ (improvement), and "these new parameters are used in the next iteration of self-play to make the search even stronger". The paper itself calls this "a policy iteration procedure".

AlphaGo Zero's loss, term by term

The network fθf_\thetafθ​ maps a board sss to (p,v)=fθ(s)(p, v) = f_\theta(s)(p,v)=fθ​(s). Training minimizes (Silver et al., eq. 1)

l=(z−v)2−π⊤log⁡p+c ∥θ∥2l = (z - v)^2 - \pi^\top \log p + c\,\lVert\theta\rVert^2 l=(z−v)2−π⊤logp+c∥θ∥2

  • (z−v)2(z - v)^2(z−v)2 is evaluation: the value output moves toward zzz, the winner of the self-play game: +1+1+1 or −1-1−1 from the current player's side.
  • −π⊤log⁡p-\pi^\top \log p−π⊤logp is improvement: the move probabilities move toward the search probabilities π\piπ, where πa∝N(s,a)1/τ\pi_a \propto N(s,a)^{1/\tau}πa​∝N(s,a)1/τ and N(s,a)N(s,a)N(s,a) counts how often the search visited move aaa.
  • c ∥θ∥2c\,\lVert\theta\rVert^2c∥θ∥2 is weight regularization.

Training started from random play and ran for about 3 days and 4.9 million self-play games, with 1,600 search simulations per move. The result beat AlphaGo Lee 100 games to 0 (Silver et al., pp. 6 and 8 of the author version).

What I take from it

Now, when I read about a new RL method, I look for the two processes. What judges the current policy? What turns that judgment into a better policy? And how far does each one go before handing over to the other: a full solve, a single sweep, one TD step, one gradient step, or a whole tree search? Most of the differences between methods in the series are answers to those three questions.
